extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in media, broadcasting policy, and US politics
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article describing the suspension of a U.S. late-night talk show and the related legal, regulatory, corporate, and political reactions. Covers how broadcasting rules, FCC authority, affiliate decisions, and free-speech concerns intersect in such incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC authority limited to obscene material
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC's authority in regulating broadcast content is largely limited to obscene material (including graphic profanity, nudity, explicit sexual content, and excessive violence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists examples of the categories the FCC can regulate and notes other limited areas of authority (advertising during children's programs, sponsorship identification, and on-air contest conduct). It emphasizes that most non-obscene speech is outside routine FCC content enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest standard for broadcast licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: "The public interest is best served by permitting free expression of views" and public-interest considerations are invoked in determining whether broadcasters meet obligations tied to holding a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece contrasts arguments that content 'not in the public interest' could threaten a license with the FCC's official position that communications policy favors permitting expression and encouraging responsive counter-speech rather than suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement threshold for news distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters are only subject to enforcement if it can be proven that they deliberately distorted a factual news report; factual inaccuracies alone are not actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to disputes over satirical or commentary programs: as a late-night entertainment talk show with satirical news commentary, it would be doubtful Jimmy Kimmel Live! falls under those enforcement rules unless deliberate news distortion were proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal time rule scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal time rules require broadcasters to provide comparable time and placement for opposing candidates, not necessarily to air programs identical to the initiating candidate's program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes criticisms invoking equal time (e.g., suggestions it could apply to The View) but clarifies the rule's limited, candidate-focused remit and that having both liberal and conservative guests does not create an equal-time violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions related to children's programming, sponsorship, and contests
rubrics_metrics.description: FCC authority includes restrictions on advertising during children's programs (including limits on product cross-promotion), sponsorship identification requirements, and rules governing the conduct of on-air contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are listed as distinct regulatory areas the FCC enforces, separate from the broader content regulation limits (obscenity/excessive violence/etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threatened punitive regulatory actions (jawboning) as First Amendment concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials' threats of punitive regulatory action — including potential revocation of broadcast licenses — to coerce disciplinary responses by broadcasters can raise First Amendment and 'jawboning' concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes criticism that FCC chairman Brendan Carr's threats to punish ABC/affiliates for Kimmel's remarks may have violated the First Amendment by pressuring private parties through regulatory menace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliate preemption rights and economic dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Local station owners and affiliates may choose to pull or preempt network programming at their discretion; networks' late-night shows may be financially dependent on affiliate fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article details Nexstar and Sinclair pulling Jimmy Kimmel Live! from ABC-affiliated stations, explains the economic importance of affiliate fees to late-night programs, and notes that preemptions can significantly reduce national coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate decision factors: employee safety, advertiser and legal risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast network and parent-company decisions (such as suspending a host) factor in employee safety, advertiser concerns, doxxing/death threats, legal exposure, and broader business/regulatory risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Disney executives reportedly considered staff safety and advertiser reaction when suspending Kimmel; the company paid crew through the suspension week and weighed potential FCC retaliation and litigation risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of political satire as a form of free speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Political satire is described as a core form of protected expression — 'one of the oldest and most important forms of free speech' — and therefore commonly targeted but legally significant in free-speech debates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes statements defending satire and notes commentators' views that satire enjoys First Amendment protection and that governmental or regulatory suppression of satire raises constitutional concerns.
